t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The aim of the session is to teach the toxicological significance and analytical methods of neutral and weakly basic substances that pass into the organic solvent in an acidic medium. The plan consists of three items. The first: the toxicological significance of phenazone, that is, antipyrine, propyphenazone, that is, amidopyrine, metamizole sodium, that is, analgin, and phenylbutazone, that is, butadione. The second: the toxicological significance of phenacetin, salicylic acid and acetylsalicylic acid. The third: the methods of their analysis, that is, TLC screening and UV spectrophotometry.

The expected outcomes are as follows. Students master the conditions for detecting phenacetin and pyrazole derivatives in pure solutions, and in a solution of unknown composition, by qualitative reactions. The results are recorded in the workbook and confirmed by the teacher. Necessary items: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual materials; the work is carried out in a specially equipped room.

t: Session map: phenacetin, salicylic acid, pyrazole
n: This is the session map. The topic includes the toxicological significance and analytical methods of phenacetin, salicylic acid, acetylsalicylic acid and pyrazole derivatives. Phenacetin is detected by its hydrolysis products: azo dye, CrO3 and nitration reactions, and also UV 250 nm. Salicylic acid is detected with iron(III) chloride, and the colour depends on pH. Antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin are distinguished with nitrite, FeCl3, AgNO3, benzoquinone and TLC. In TLC they give characteristic coloured spots in the range Rf = 0.15–0.17.

This slide gives laboratory sessions 3 and 4 of the DVSSM course. Session 3: analysis of phenacetin, salicylic and acetylsalicylic acids in the extract; quantitative analysis is carried out by the photoelectric colorimeter (PEC) method. Session 4: analysis in the extract of pyrazole derivatives, that is, antipyrine, amidopyrine, analgin and butadione, using TLC screening and UV spectrophotometry. In session 3 the results are recorded in the workbook and confirmed by the teacher.

Properties and significance of phenacetin. Phenacetin is a white crystalline powder, sparingly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents. It has antipyretic, analgesic and anti-cold action. In a large dose it can cause methaemoglobinaemia, anaemia and nephritis. In the body it is hydrolysed to form p-aminophenol, which is oxidised to quinonimine. If hydrolysis is incomplete, the highly toxic n-phenetidine is formed.

t: Detecting phenacetin by the azo dye reaction
n: Detecting phenacetin by the azo dye reaction. On hydrolysis a primary aromatic amine is formed, so the azo dye reaction is used. Procedure: 1–2 drops are evaporated, heated with 1 ml of conc. HCl, after cooling 1% NaNO2 is added, then alkaline β-naphthol is added. Result: the solution turns red. Task: write the chemical equation of the reaction.

Reactions of phenacetin with chromic anhydride and nitration. With chromic anhydride: 5–6 drops of the chloroform solution are dried, boiled with 1 ml of conc. HCl for 5 minutes, and after cooling 2% CrO3 is added. Result: dark red colour from oxidation of p-aminophenol. In nitration, if 20% nitric acid is added to the residue and heated, nitrophenacetin is formed and a yellow-brown colour appears.

Phenacetin can also be detected by its UV spectrum and microcrystals. A solution of phenacetin in ethyl alcohol absorbs UV rays maximally at a wavelength of 250 nm. In addition, phenacetin forms characteristic microcrystals with the copper–iodine complex. The amount is determined by the photocolorimetric method based on the azo dye reaction, that is, with the PEC or a spectrophotometer.

UV spectrum maxima. A solution of phenacetin in ethyl alcohol absorbs UV rays maximally at 250 nm. A solution of salicylic acid in 0.5 N NaOH absorbs maximally at 300 nm, and in 0.1 N H2SO4 at 302 nm. A solution of analgin in 0.1 N HCl absorbs maximally at 258 nm. Remember these four values.

We compare phenacetin and salicylic acid. Phenacetin is a neutral white crystalline powder, sparingly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents. It is detected by its hydrolysis products, that is, the azo dye, CrO3 and nitration reactions, UV maximum 250 nm. Salicylic acid has acidic properties, is poorly soluble in cold water, very soluble in hot water and melts at 159 °C. It is detected through complexes with the iron ion: Fe(III) chloride gives a green-violet colour. UV maxima 300 nm, in 0.5 N NaOH, and 302 nm, in 0.1 N H2SO4.

Properties of salicylic acid. It forms small, needle-like, light, odourless crystals with a sour-sweet taste. It is poorly soluble in cold water, very soluble in hot water, readily soluble in alcohol and ether and melts at 159 °C. Salicylic acid is distilled with steam, so it can also be isolated from a biological object by steam. It is used to make drugs such as aspirin and salol. Its use for preserving foodstuffs has been abolished by the state.

Poisoning with salicylic acid and metabolism. In poisoning, headache, dizziness, ringing in the ears and reduced hearing, diarrhoea, vomiting and collapse are observed. The acid is quickly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the blood. Mainly, that is 80%, it is excreted through the kidneys and is entirely eliminated within 24 hours. The remaining 20% undergoes metabolism in the tissues, forming dihydroxybenzoic and trihydroxybenzoic acids. It is isolated from the object with polar solvents in an acidic medium.

Uses of salicylic acid. Salicylic acid is used mainly in medicine and the pharmaceutical industry to make drugs such as aspirin and salol. It was also used for preserving foodstuffs, but because of its toxic action this has been abolished by the state. Therefore, foodstuffs may also be sent to the forensic chemistry laboratory as physical evidence in order to detect it.

t: Salicylic acid: reaction with iron(III) chloride
n: The reaction of salicylic acid with iron(III) chloride. Salicylic acid forms a green-violet colour with iron(III) chloride. It is important that the composition and colour of the complex depend on pH. At pH 1.8–2.5, monosalicylate forms and the colour is bluish-pink. At pH 4–8, disalicylate forms and the colour is red-brown. At pH 8–11, trisalicylate forms and the colour is yellow.

Features of the Fe(III) reaction. The reaction is characteristic in the absence of substances that bind the phenolic hydroxyl, for example maltol. The colour formed is not discharged by alcohol, which distinguishes it from phenol. Bromine water, in the presence of salicylic acid, gives a white precipitate, that is, tribromophenol, and CO2 is released, but this reaction is not specific for salicylic acid. The sensitivity of the bromine water reaction is 1:40000; a negative result shows the absence of salicylic acid.

t: Other methods of detecting salicylic acid
n: Other methods of detecting salicylic acid. When heated with methyl alcohol and concentrated sulphuric acid, the characteristic smell of methyl salicylate is noticed; ethyl alcohol may also be used instead of methyl. In the UV spectrum, its solution in 0.5 N NaOH absorbs maximally at 300 nm and its solution in 0.1 N H2SO4 at 302 nm. The amount is determined by titration with alkali, by the bromatometric method or by UV spectrophotometry.

We summarise the methods of detecting salicylic acid. With iron(III) chloride, a pH-dependent colour forms; with bromine water, a precipitate of tribromophenol. The smell of methyl salicylate and the UV spectrum maxima, that is, 300 and 302 nm, are also used. In blood and urine, Trinder's reagent and Fe(NO3)3 are used for the preliminary examination. The sensitivity of the bromine water reaction for salicylic acid is 1:40000.

t: Preliminary testing of blood and urine for salicylic acid
n: Preliminary testing of blood and urine for salicylic acid. If Trinder's reagent, that is, HgCl2 and Fe(NO3)3, is added to urine or blood serum, a red-scarlet colour forms in the presence of salicylic acid. A red-scarlet colour also forms if a solution of iron(III) nitrate in nitric acid is dropped into urine or blood serum. Both reactions are recommended for the preliminary examination.

Pyrazole derivatives. These include phenazone, that is, antipyrine, propyphenazone, that is, amidopyrine, metamizole sodium, that is, analgin, and phenylbutazone, that is, butadione. In the session, antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin are detected in a pure and in an unknown solution. In the table each trade name is given with its chemical name: antipyrine corresponds to phenazone, amidopyrine to propyphenazone, analgin to metamizole sodium, and butadione to phenylbutazone.

Significance and metabolism of antipyrine. Antipyrine is an antipyretic and analgesic; it is a colourless crystal, readily soluble in water, alcohol and chloroform. It is quickly absorbed from the digestive organs, reaching maximum concentration in the blood within 1–2 hours. 30–40% combines with glucuronic acid and is excreted as the glucuronide, part becomes 4-hydroxyantipyrine, and 5% is excreted unchanged in the urine.

Amidopyrine and analgin. The toxicological significance of amidopyrine is similar to that of antipyrine. In the body it is converted into 4-aminoantipyrine, methylaminoantipyrine, red rubazonic acid and methylrubazonic acid. Therefore the urine of a person who has taken a large dose turns red. The use and toxicological significance of analgin are also similar to those of antipyrine.

t: Antipyrine and amidopyrine: reaction with nitrite
n: The reaction of antipyrine and amidopyrine with nitrite. To 1 ml of solution, a few drops of 10% sulphuric acid and 2–3 drops of saturated NaNO2 are added. Antipyrine gives a blue-green colour, whereas amidopyrine gives violet. The violet colour of amidopyrine fades in excess nitrite, and a blue-green colour appears. Antipyrine with β-naphthylamine gives a red pyrazolone dye.

t: Antipyrine: nitroso derivative and pyrazolone dye
n: Antipyrine: nitroso derivative and pyrazolone dye. With sodium nitrite in an acidic medium, antipyrine forms green nitrosoantipyrine. If there is a lot of antipyrine, a green precipitate may fall. If β-naphthylamine is allowed to act on nitrosoantipyrine, a red pyrazolone dye is formed. The reaction proceeds in an acidic medium in the presence of NaNO2 and HCl.

Oxidation of amidopyrine and its reaction with chromotropic acid. Amidopyrine is oxidised to reddish oxyamidopyrine; red urine arises from the oxidation products of amidopyrine. Concentrated H2SO4 decomposes amidopyrine, forming formaldehyde. Formaldehyde gives a pink colour with chromotropic acid.

We compare antipyrine and amidopyrine. With nitrite in H2SO4 medium, antipyrine gives blue-green and amidopyrine violet. With FeCl3, antipyrine gives red, that is, ferripyrine, and amidopyrine violet; the colour disappears in excess of the reagent. Antipyrine forms a red dye with β-naphthylamine. Amidopyrine reduces silver nitrate, giving a pink colour and a black precipitate, and with sulphuric and chromotropic acid it gives a pink colour.

Toxicological significance of pyrazole derivatives. Antipyrine is an antipyretic and analgesic; applied locally it has a haemostatic property. The toxicological significance of amidopyrine is similar to that of antipyrine, and red urine is associated with rubazone. The use and toxicological significance of analgin are similar to antipyrine; it can be detected with benzoquinone by the PEC method.

t: Antipyrine and amidopyrine: FeCl3 and AgNO3
n: Tests with FeCl3 and AgNO3. If 0.5 ml of 5% iron(III) chloride is added to 1 ml of solution, antipyrine gives a red colour, that is, ferripyrine, and amidopyrine gives violet. The colour disappears under the action of an excess of the reagent. Also, if 3–5 drops of 1% AgNO3 are added to 1 ml of solution and heated on a water bath for 3–5 minutes, a violet colour indicates amidopyrine.

Reactions of analgin. With a solution of benzoquinone in acetic acid, analgin forms a cherry-red product. Under the action of iron(III) chloride, a violet product that quickly fades appears. With Nessler's reagent, a red-yellow precipitate; with chloramine B and dilute HCl, a yellow colour. With KIO3 and HCl, a red colour appears, and in excess of the reagent a dark red and brown precipitate.

The UV spectrum of analgin. A solution of analgin in 0.1 N hydrochloric acid absorbs maximally at a wavelength of 258 nm. The DVSSM course package gives the same value: 258 nm in 0.1 N HCl. The amount of analgin is determined by the PEC method from the colour formed with benzoquinone.

The working procedure of the TLC method. On the starting line, alcoholic solutions of antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin are applied at 1 cm intervals. The chamber is saturated with acetone–chloroform, in the ratio 1:9, and the plate is placed in the chamber. When the system has risen 10 cm, the plate is removed, dried at room temperature and sprayed with FeCl3 solution.

The sequence of TLC stages, by the blitz method. Task: to arrange the stages of detecting analgin by TLC in the correct sequence, 12 stages in total. First the preparation: choosing the plate, the starting line, the solvent system, saturating the chamber and applying the extract. Then placing the plate in the chamber, rising 10 cm, marking the front line, spraying and determining Rf. Rf is calculated by the formula Rf = a / b.

TLC results and Rf. In the range Rf = 0.15–0.17, characteristic coloured spots form. Antipyrine gives a red spot, amidopyrine violet, and analgin a blue spot. When sprayed with Dragendorff's reagent, analgin gives a brown spot; the result is compared with the spot of the standard substance. Rf = a / b, where a is the distance from the starting line to the centre of the spot, and b is the distance from the starting line to the finish line.

Quantitative determination of pyrazole derivatives. Antipyrine forms a precipitate with picric acid, and the excess picric acid is titrated. Another method is UV spectrophotometry. Amidopyrine is determined by the extraction-photometric method on the basis of its complex with bromophenol blue. Amidopyrine gives a pink colour with sulphuric and chromotropic acid, owing to the formation of formaldehyde in concentrated H2SO4.

Situational problems. The first: when HgCl2 and Fe(NO3)3 were added to the urine of N., born in 2009, a red-scarlet colour formed; determine by which substance the poisoning occurred and write its full analysis. The second: on a cold day, a patient took many bitter drugs, and the urine is red-brown; when H2SO4 and chromotropic acid were added to the extract, a pink colour formed. The third, case 16: state the procedure for isolating the substance from the object and the chemical-toxicological analysis.

Case 17. A 10 ml urine sample has been delivered for forensic chemical examination; the colour of the urine is red. There are signs of nephritis in the kidneys, and the blood analysis showed methaemoglobinaemia. Task: to set out for which substances analysis is necessary and to carry out the forensic chemical analysis.

Review questions. First: why does phenacetin pass into the organic solvent layer in an acidic medium, and what is its toxicological significance. Second: write the equations of the reactions of phenacetin forming the azo dye, with chromic anhydride and forming nitrosophenacetin. Third: what products do antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin form with iron(III) chloride, and can they be distinguished. Fourth: if amidopyrine is stored beyond its expiry, what structural change may it undergo; explain with the formula.

Continuation of the review questions. Can phenacetin be detected by TLC? Which substances are pyrazole derivatives, and what are their toxicological and narcological significance? What products do pyrazole derivatives form with nitrous acid, and can they be distinguished? Which reagents can be used in detecting pyrazole derivatives by TLC? What other reactions are used in detecting pyrazole derivatives?

We conclude. Phenacetin is detected by its hydrolysis products: azo dye, dark red colour with CrO3, nitration; UV 250 nm. Salicylic acid gives a pH-dependent colour with Fe(III); UV maxima 300 and 302 nm. Antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin are distinguished with nitrite, FeCl3, AgNO3, benzoquinone and TLC, with Rf = 0.15–0.17 in TLC.
